title: How to choose a first emergency fund target you can actually track
excerpt: Build a starting cash-buffer plan around a specific expense, a manageable contribution and a clear review date, with a worked example.
body:
A savings target is easier to use when it answers a concrete question: what would this money allow me to handle without reorganizing every other bill? Instead of starting with someone else's impressive account balance, start with one disruption you want to prepare for.

Separate surprises from predictable bills

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes emergency savings as money reserved for unexpected costs and says the appropriate amount depends on the household. It also highlights access, safety and a repeatable savings habit. That is a useful starting point, rather than a universal amount everyone must reach.

On a blank page, make two columns. Put routine costs with known due dates in the first. Put plausible disruptions in the second. A yearly subscription belongs in the first column even if it feels inconvenient. An urgent, unplanned repair belongs in the second. This exercise is a planning aid, not a definition that overrides your circumstances.

A worked first-target example

Suppose you choose an illustrative first target of 600 currency units. You already have 150 available for that purpose and can set aside 75 each month. The remaining gap is 450; dividing it by 75 gives six monthly contributions. This example ignores interest and assumes no withdrawals.

Illustrative cash-buffer plan
ItemAmount
Chosen target600
Starting savings150
Remaining gap450
Monthly contribution75

Make the plan easy to review

Write down the target, what the fund is for, and the date of your next check-in. If a contribution would make an essential bill difficult to pay, change the contribution rather than treating the example as an obligation. The CFPB cautions that automatic transfers should be planned around available balances to avoid overdrafts.

At each review, record the actual balance beside the planned balance. A difference is information: perhaps a cost occurred, income changed, or the contribution was too ambitious. You can revise the next step without pretending the original plan was a promise.

After you use the money

Keep a short note of the withdrawal and recalculate the gap. For example, a 120 withdrawal from a 600 balance leaves 480. Returning to 600 at 60 per month takes two contributions if there is no interest or further spending. The arithmetic stays simple; the target should remain yours.

For longer-term illustrations, try the savings calculator. For the assumptions behind its results, read our monthly compounding guide.

title: Monthly compound interest explained: a savings example you can check
excerpt: Follow the arithmetic behind a monthly savings projection, separate contributions from interest, and understand what a calculator leaves out.
body:
A future savings balance combines two different things: money you put in and growth calculated from the assumptions you choose. Seeing the split makes a calculator more useful than looking at a single large number.

Start with explicit assumptions

Investor.gov's compound interest calculator asks for an initial amount, regular contributions, a time horizon, an estimated rate and compounding frequency. Our tool uses monthly compounding and deposits at the end of each month. Those choices matter when comparing its results with a different calculator.

Consider an illustrative starting balance of 1,000, a monthly contribution of 100, a nominal annual rate of 5%, and a ten-year period. These are hypothetical inputs in one consistent currency, not a rate offer or an investment forecast. Taxes, fees, inflation and withdrawals are excluded.

Check the first two months

The monthly rate is 0.05 divided by 12. After month one, the balance is 1,000 multiplied by (1 + 0.05/12), plus 100: approximately 1,104.17. Applying the same calculation to the unrounded balance gives approximately 1,208.77 after month two.

The calculation keeps its internal precision and rounds only the display. Rounding the balance after every intermediate step can produce a slightly different result over a long period. A bank's actual accrual and crediting conventions may also differ from this simplified model.

Separate deposits from calculated growth

Ten-year illustration with end-of-month deposits
MeasureAmount
Initial deposit1,000.00
120 contributions of 10012,000.00
Total contributed13,000.00
Calculated interest4,175.24
Projected balance17,175.24

Try a zero-rate comparison

With the same deposits and no interest, the ending balance is exactly 13,000. That comparison shows how much of this scenario comes from saving rather than from the assumed rate. It also provides a useful check: if a zero-rate calculation produces interest, something is wrong with the inputs or formula.

Use scenarios, not promises

Change one input at a time and label each result. Doubling the contribution changes your own cash commitment; increasing the assumed rate changes a modelling assumption. They are not interchangeable actions. This calculator does not model losses or varying rates, so it cannot represent every investment outcome.

Try the calculator and yearly CSV breakdown. If the money is intended for near-term surprises, also consider the purpose of an emergency cash buffer before treating a long-term projection as a plan.

title: How to compare investment fees without overlooking the small print
excerpt: Use a simple comparison worksheet to distinguish ongoing, transaction and account charges, with an illustrative calculation of fee drag.
body:
Two investments can use similar language while charging for different things. A useful comparison begins with the documents, the charging basis and the holding period, not with the smallest number in a headline.

Identify the different charges

The SEC's Investor.gov bulletin distinguishes charges associated with transactions from ongoing costs. It explains that fund expenses can be reflected in returns and that other account or advice fees may apply separately. Read the relevant disclosure documents rather than assuming one displayed percentage includes everything.

Make a worksheet with one row per product and columns for the fee name, how it is calculated, when it is charged, and where you found it. Record missing information as a question, not as zero. This is an organizational approach you can use before deciding whether two products are actually comparable.

Compare like with like

Questions for a fee comparison worksheet
ChargeQuestion to record
Percentage-based ongoing feeWhich assets or balance does the percentage apply to?
Transaction chargeDoes it apply when buying, selling, or both?
Fixed account chargeIs it monthly, quarterly or annual?
Exit or transfer costWhat would moving or withdrawing the investment cost?

A flat 30 annual charge represents 3% of a 1,000 balance but 0.3% of a 10,000 balance. That arithmetic does not say which account is suitable. It shows why the amount you expect to hold belongs in the comparison.

An illustration of ongoing fee drag

Consider 10,000 held for 20 years, with no further deposits and a hypothetical 5% annual return before fees. In a simplified model, subtract the annual percentage fee from that return before compounding. At a 0.25% fee, the illustration ends near 25,298; at a 1% fee, it ends near 21,911. Both are calculated examples, not expected returns.

Understand what the illustration leaves out

Real charges may be deducted at different times, returns change, and deposits or withdrawals alter the balance. The SEC emphasizes that fees reduce money available to grow. Our example isolates that effect while deliberately holding everything else constant.

Cost is one part of a decision. A cheaper product can still have a different objective, risk, access restriction or service level. Record those differences beside the fee comparison, and ask for clarification where a disclosure is unclear. Do not treat this worksheet as a recommendation to buy or sell a particular investment.

To understand the arithmetic behind constant-rate projections, read our compound interest guide. Use the contact form to flag an error in this explanation.
